uncited: Ray generation and camera models define the mapping from 2D image coordinates to 3D rays, establishing the geometric foundation for volume rendering by determining which parts of the scene are observed.
This family solves the problem of translating pixel locations into valid ray origins and directions for subsequent intersection and integration steps.

It is distinguished from sibling topics like [Ray-primitive intersection](769-ray-primitive-intersection.md) by focusing solely on the creation of the ray bundle rather than the traversal of geometry, and from [Parallel and GPU primitives](771-parallel-and-gpu-primitives.md) by defining the logical camera parameters rather than the execution strategy.
All methods in this family generate a set of rays, typically represented as a `RayBundle` containing origins $\mathbf{o}$ and directions $\mathbf{d}$, for every pixel in the output image.
**Coordinate Mapping**: Converting discrete pixel indices $(u, v)$ or normalized device coordinates (NDC) into continuous 2D positions on a virtual image plane.
**Camera Basis Construction**: Defining a local coordinate system for the camera using an eye position $\mathbf{e}$, a target point $\mathbf{t}$, and an up vector $\mathbf{up}$.
This yields the basis vectors: forward $\mathbf{f}$, right $\mathbf{r}$, and camera-up $\mathbf{u}$.
**Ray Assembly**: Computing the origin $\mathbf{o}$ (often the eye position or a point on the image plane) and the direction $\mathbf{d}$ (normalized vector from origin to image plane point).
The mathematical consistency requires that the generated rays correctly project the 3D scene onto the 2D image plane according to the chosen projection model (perspective or orthographic).
Historically, ray generation has evolved from simple parallel beam projections (used in early tomography) to complex perspective models.
Modern implementations, such as those found in differentiable tomography libraries, often automate camera parameter computation.
A common pitfall in camera basis construction is the singularity when the forward vector is parallel to the up vector, causing the cross product for the 'right' vector to become zero.

This matches the claim's formulas and variable definitions exactly.
